title: The Study of Quasi-Periodic Pulsations in Solar and Stellar Flares with SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Nakariakov01. Advancing Astrophysics with SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: An intensively studied phenomenon which is not described by the standard flare model are quasi-periodic pulsations (QPP) of the flaring emission. As analysis of the QPP phenomenon intrinsically requires a combination of high time and spatial resolutions, especially in the radio band, the unprecedented capabilities of SKA offer us a unique opportunity to reach a breakthrough progress in the observational study of QPP. The SKA-Mid-frequency band falls in a unique window where both coherent emissions from particle acceleration sites and incoherent gyrosynchrotron emissions from non-thermal particles in coronal loops can be studied. With an additional polarisation dimension and the capability to perform wideband spectroscopic imaging, the QPPs in gyrosynchrotron emission ($\ge 1$~GHz) and plasma emission will help understand the local magnetic field modulation due to active phenomena and the response seen in the particle acceleration observable below ~600~MHz. An incomplete list of specific science questions to be addressed with SKA includes (a) the role of QPP in the energy partition in flares, (b) seismology of flaring sites by QPP of different classes, (c ) differences and similarities between QPP in solar and stellar flares, (d) advancing the standard flare model, (e) the physics of repetitive magnetic reconnection: spontaneous vs induced, (f) ML techniques in the detection, classification and analysis of QPP, (g) QPP in weak flares. The latter topic could be especially advanced with SKA which will allow for high-cadence high fidelity radio imaging of weak energy release events.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), particularly its Mid-frequency band, can advance the observational study of quasi-periodic pulsations (QPP) in solar flares. SKA's high time and spatial resolution, wideband spectroscopic imaging, and polarimetric capabilities enable investigation of QPP in gyrosynchrotron and plasma emission, addressing questions on energy partition, flare seismology, solar-stellar flare comparisons, the standard flare model, repetitive magnetic reconnection, ML techniques, and QPP in weak flares.
AI.motivation: QPP is an intensively studied phenomenon not described by the standard flare model. Its analysis requires high time and spatial resolution (especially in radio), and SKA's unprecedented capabilities offer a unique opportunity to achieve breakthrough progress in the observational study of QPP.
AI.method: The paper proposes leveraging the SKA-Mid-frequency band, which covers a unique window where both coherent emissions from particle acceleration sites and incoherent gyrosynchrotron emissions from non-thermal particles in coronal loops can be studied. It utilizes additional polarisation dimensions and wideband spectroscopic imaging to study QPPs in gyrosynchrotron emission (≥1 GHz) and plasma emission (below ~600 MHz) to probe local magnetic field modulation and particle acceleration.
AI.result: The paper identifies a list of specific science questions to be addressed with SKA, including QPP's role in energy partition in flares, seismology of flaring sites, differences/similarities between solar and stellar flare QPPs, advancing the standard flare model, physics of repetitive magnetic reconnection, ML techniques for QPP detection/classification/analysis, and QPP in weak flares—the latter being particularly advanced by SKA's high-cadence, high-fidelity radio imaging of weak energy release events.
AI.conclusion: SKA offers a unique observational window to make breakthrough progress in QPP research, potentially improving the standard flare model and enabling study of weak flares that have been difficult to observe at high fidelity.

title: PANTERA. I. Hunting for the Most Metal-Rich Stars in the Solar Neighborhood with High-Resolution Spectroscopy
summary: We present PANTERA (Project for Astrophysical Nucleosynthesis and Targeted Exploration of metal-Rich Abundances), a high-resolution spectroscopic survey of the most metal-rich stars in the solar neighborhood. In this first paper, we report iron abundances for 56 metal-rich stars, selected from Gaia DR3 XP spectrophotometric metallicities. These targets were observed with the PEPSI spectrograph on the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT), the Levy spectrograph on the Automated Planet Finder (APF) telescope, and the HIRES spectrograph on the Keck telescope. We measure [Fe/H] from an equivalent-width analysis of iron lines, with the effective temperature taken from photometry and the surface gravity from the Gaia parallax. We verify our measurement using Gaia benchmark stars, observing some sources with more than one spectrograph, using a second synthesis code, and an independent equivalent-width measurement. We find that the Gaia-XP metallicities over-predict [Fe/H] for part of our sample: they are consistent for the dwarfs, though a selection bias limits what the dwarf agreement can show, and reach $0.16\pm0.02$ dex for the cool giants. We attribute the over-prediction in part to the strong blue line blanketing of the cool metal-rich giants and to the survey labels on which the XP metallicities were trained. We also found 25 of the 56 stars to be ultra-metal-rich ([Fe/H] $> 0.4$), with the most iron-rich stars reaching [Fe/H]$=+0.58$. We discuss the implications of our result on studying metal-rich populations.

AI.tldr: PANTERA is a high-resolution spectroscopic survey targeting the most metal-rich stars in the solar neighborhood. In this first paper, 56 metal-rich stars observed with PEPSI/LBT, Levy/APF, and HIRES/Keck are analyzed for iron abundances via equivalent-width analysis. Gaia XP metallicities are found to over-predict [Fe/H] for cool giants by up to 0.16±0.02 dex (partly due to blue line blanketing and training labels), while agreeing for dwarfs. 25 of 56 stars are ultra-metal-rich ([Fe/H]>0.4), with the most iron-rich reaching +0.58.
AI.motivation: To characterize the most metal-rich stars in the solar neighborhood at high spectral resolution, since these extreme objects constrain nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution models at the high-metallicity end, yet remain poorly studied due to the difficulty of discovering and characterizing them.
AI.method: Stars were selected from Gaia DR3 XP spectrophotometric metallicities and observed with three high-resolution spectrographs (PEPSI on LBT, Levy on APF, HIRES on Keck). [Fe/H] was measured using equivalent-width analysis of iron lines, with photometric effective temperatures and Gaia-parallax-based surface gravities. The measurements were validated through Gaia benchmark stars, cross-observations with multiple spectrographs, a second synthesis code, and independent equivalent-width measurements.
AI.result: Gaia XP metallicities over-predict [Fe/H] for part of the sample: they are consistent for dwarfs (though a selection bias limits the demonstration), and over-predict by 0.16±0.02 dex for cool giants. 25 of 56 stars are ultra-metal-rich ([Fe/H]>0.4), with the most iron-rich reaching [Fe/H]=+0.58.
AI.conclusion: The over-prediction in cool giants is attributed to strong blue line blanketing and to the survey labels on which XP metallicities were trained. The findings have implications for studying metal-rich populations, particularly highlighting biases in photometric metallicity estimates and the existence of a population of ultra-metal-rich stars in the solar neighborhood.
